examples: The team embraced the new design system faster than I expected.
We should embrace ambiguity in discovery instead of rushing to solutions.
Leadership has fully embraced the mobile-first strategy.
meaning: To accept an idea, change, or approach willingly and with enthusiasm.
tip: At work it is almost always about ideas or change, not hugging people: 'embrace change / feedback / a new process'.

examples: Is it feasible to ship the redesign before the Q4 freeze?
The engineers said the animation is feasible but costly.
Let's check what's feasible for the MVP and park the rest.
meaning: Possible to do with the time, money, and resources available.
tip: Pair: 'technically feasible', 'a feasibility check'. Stronger and more concrete than 'possible'.

examples: I think you misconstrued my comment; I was praising the layout, not criticizing it.
Please don't misconstrue the short reply as disinterest, I was between meetings.
Her silence in the review was misconstrued as disagreement.
meaning: To understand something wrongly, usually because you read a hidden meaning into it.
tip: Formal and slightly stronger than 'misunderstand'; often used when someone takes offence that wasn't intended.

examples: The team misinterpreted the metric and optimized for the wrong thing.
Users might misinterpret the red badge as an error rather than a notification.
Let me restate the goal so nobody misinterprets it.
meaning: To explain or understand the meaning of something incorrectly.
tip: Very common at work: 'misinterpret the data / the brief / the feedback'.

examples: We overestimated how many users would finish onboarding on day one.
It's easy to overestimate the engineering effort for a small UI change.
I don't want to overestimate the impact, but early numbers look good.
meaning: To think something is bigger, better, or more likely than it really is.
tip: Opposite: underestimate. Common idiom: 'I can't overestimate how important X is' = it is extremely important.

examples: I presume the API is ready, since nobody flagged a blocker.
Don't presume users will scroll; test it.
I presumed you had seen the Figma link, sorry about that.
meaning: To suppose something is true because it seems likely, without proof.

sentences.corrected: Guys, I've got the A/B test results and now I presume the problem roots in the backend, not the frontend.
sentences.text: Guys, I've got the A/B test results and now I presume that problem roots in backend, not frontend

tip: Slightly more formal than 'assume'; 'I presume' is a polite way to check an assumption.

examples: Admittedly, the first prototype was rough, but it got the idea across.
The flow is, admittedly, longer than I'd like.
Admittedly I missed that edge case in the spec.
meaning: Used to agree that something is true, often before a 'but'.
tip: Great softener in reviews: concede a point first, then make your argument.

examples: The spacing in this screen is all over the place.
My notes are all over the place, give me a minute to find it.
Dark patterns are all over the place in subscription apps.
meaning: Disorganized or inconsistent; also, present everywhere.
tip: Negative when describing work: 'the brief was all over the place' = confusing. Neutral when meaning 'everywhere'.

examples: The offsite helped me bond with the people on the platform team.
It takes a few sprints to bond with a new squad.
Users bond with products that remember their preferences.
meaning: To build a close, trusting relationship with someone.

sentences.corrected: You should bond with our frontend engineer Mike.
sentences.text: You need to bond with our frontend engineer Mike

sentences.corrected: You should bond with Joe, he's a developer in our team.
sentences.text: You have to bond with Joe, he's a developer in our team

tip: Noun: 'a bond'. 'Team bonding' is the HR phrase for activities that build this.

examples: Bottoms up, team, we shipped!
We took a bottom-up approach: talked to support agents first, then designed.
Component libraries usually grow bottom-up from real screens.
meaning: Said before drinking together ('cheers'); as 'bottom-up', an approach that starts from details or from the people doing the work.
tip: 'Bottoms up!' is the toast. 'Bottom-up' (hyphen, no s) is the strategy word; opposite 'top-down'.

examples: I was channeling my old design lead when I pushed back on the deadline.
In that presentation she was channeling Steve Jobs, pauses and all.
Try channeling the user's frustration when you write the error copy.
meaning: To behave or speak like a particular person, as if their spirit were acting through you.
tip: Playful and informal. Also literal 'channel energy / resources into X' = direct them.

examples: The modal conceals the main content, which confuses first-time users.
He didn't conceal his frustration with the timeline.
Advanced settings are concealed behind a 'More' toggle.
meaning: To hide something so it is not seen or known.
tip: More formal than 'hide'. 'Reveal' is the opposite, and both are common in UI talk: 'reveal on hover'.

examples: A long migration project is a test of endurance more than brilliance.
Her endurance through three rounds of stakeholder feedback impressed everyone.
Endurance matters in design: most wins come from iterating, not one big idea.
meaning: The ability to keep going through something difficult or long.
tip: Verb: 'endure'. Related: 'stamina', 'resilience' (bouncing back) is slightly different.

examples: Once the headphones went on I was locked in for three hours.
We're locked in to this vendor until the contract ends next year.
The team was locked in during the final week before launch.
meaning: Fully focused and committed; also, unable to change a decision or contract.
tip: Two senses: focused (informal, newer) and contractually stuck ('vendor lock-in').

examples: Design and engineering here work on a basis of mutual respect.
Good feedback culture starts with mutual respect, not with templates.
We disagreed on the approach, but there was absolutely mutual respect.
meaning: Respect that two people or groups feel for each other equally.
tip: 'Mutual' = shared both ways: 'mutual trust', 'mutual benefit', 'the feeling is mutual'.

examples: I'll pass your feedback on to the backend team.
She passed that habit on to her kids.
Can you pass the Figma link on to the new designer?
heard: she passed that to my mom
meaning: To give or hand over something (an object, a skill, a message) to another person.

sentences.corrected: About the project - yesterday I passed all the details on to Jake, so he can work on it until the end of the week.
sentences.text: About the project - yesterday I pass all details on to Jake, so he starts until the end of the week

tip: At work: 'pass on feedback / a message / a request'. Also 'pass on' can mean 'decline': 'I'll pass on dessert'.

examples: Engineering time is precious this quarter, so let's prioritize ruthlessly.
Don't waste the user's precious attention on a welcome screen.
Those first customer calls gave us precious insight.
meaning: Very valuable and not to be wasted; also, loved and important.
tip: Warning: 'being precious about something' means being overly fussy or protective of it.

examples: I honestly didn't think we'd pull off the launch in two weeks, but we did.
She pulled off a great demo despite the broken staging build.
If we pull this off, it'll be the biggest release of the year.
meaning: To succeed at something difficult, often against expectations.
tip: Informal praise: 'You pulled it off!' Not to be confused with 'pull out' (withdraw).

examples: Calling it 'just a settings page' is a bit reductive; it handles billing too.
That summary feels reductive; the research showed more nuance.
I don't want to be reductive, but the core problem is onboarding.
meaning: Making something seem simpler than it really is, in a way that loses important detail.
tip: Useful, polite pushback: 'That's a bit reductive' = you are oversimplifying.

examples: There's some redundancy between the two menus; users see the same links twice.
We added redundancy to the backup system so one failure won't take us down.
The company announced redundancies in the sales team.
meaning: Something that is repeated or no longer needed; in the UK it also means losing your job because the role is cut.
tip: Adjective 'redundant' is what you'll hear most: 'this button is redundant'. The noun is 'redundancy', not 'redundance'.

examples: The layout should work regardless of the device it sits on.
Regardless of the outcome, the research was worth doing.
We ship on Thursday regardless of whether the dark mode is ready.
heard: Regardless of the device this sits on
meaning: Without being affected by; no matter what.
tip: 'Regardless of' takes a noun or '-ing'; 'regardless' alone can end a sentence: 'We'll ship regardless.'

examples: In payments, the room for error is tiny.
Let's build in some room for error with a confirmation step.
There's no room for error on the launch date.
meaning: How much mistake can happen without serious consequences.

sentences.corrected: Don't be so judgmental—everyone at the company, including our boss, should have room for error.
sentences.text: Don't be so judgy, here's room for error for every person at company including our boss

tip: Also 'margin for error'. 'Leave room for X' is a related everyday phrase.

examples: Your read on the user's frustration was spot on.
The estimate was spot on; we finished the day we said.
Spot on, that's exactly the problem I was trying to name.
meaning: Exactly right or accurate.
tip: Informal and warm; a great way to agree in a meeting. British in origin, understood everywhere.

examples: Three onboarding screens seems to be the sweet spot between clarity and speed.
We're trying to find the sweet spot between density and readability.
That pricing tier hit the sweet spot for small teams.
meaning: The best possible combination or balance, where everything works well.

sentences.corrected: If we can make it 5% better, it will hit the sweet spot for us.
sentences.text: If we can make it 5% better it will be a sweet spot for us

tip: Collocations: 'hit / find the sweet spot between X and Y'.

examples: I know you're extremely busy, so thank you for your time and energy today.
Thanks for your time, I'll follow up with the summary by tomorrow.
Thank you for your time; this was really helpful.
heard: you're extremely busy, thank you for your energy and your time
meaning: A polite way to close a meeting or message, acknowledging someone's effort.

sentences.corrected: I really appreciate our conversation, thank you for your time and see you next week
sentences.text: I really appreciate our conversation, thank you for your time and see you next week

tip: Ending a call with this sounds natural and professional. Add a concrete follow-up to sound even more fluent.

examples: The bulk of the work is in the edge cases, not the happy path.
We spent the bulk of the sprint on accessibility fixes.
The bulk of our users are on iOS.
meaning: The largest part or majority of something.
tip: Slightly more formal than 'most of'. Takes a noun: 'the bulk of the budget'.

examples: Let's see how the experiment plays out before we change the roadmap.
The migration played out better than our worst-case plan.
I can see how this would play out in a real sales conversation.
meaning: To develop or happen over time in a particular way.
tip: Common in strategy talk: 'how this plays out', 'play out a scenario'.

examples: A clear pattern emerged from the interviews: people skip the tutorial.
New requirements keep emerging halfway through the sprint.
She emerged as the natural lead on the project.
meaning: To appear or become known, often gradually.
tip: Noun 'emergence'; adjective 'emerging' as in 'emerging market'. Formal register.

examples: There's some ambiguity in the ticket about who owns the empty state.
Senior designers are expected to be comfortable with ambiguity.
Let's remove the ambiguity by defining 'done' for this story.
meaning: The state of having more than one possible meaning; lack of clarity.
tip: Adjective 'ambiguous'. 'Comfortable with ambiguity' appears in nearly every senior job description.

examples: The demo blew the client away.
I was blown away by how fast the new hire picked up the codebase.
Their attention to detail blows me away every time.
meaning: To impress someone enormously.

sentences.corrected: Jonathan's concept of the main page just blew me away, you have to check this out
sentences.text: The Johnatan's concept of the main paige just blow me away, you have to check this out

tip: Usually passive: 'I was blown away'. Very positive and informal.

examples: How's the prototype coming along?
A better tool came along, so we switched.
Want to come along to the user interview on Friday?
meaning: To arrive or appear; to make progress; or to join someone going somewhere.

sentences.corrected: Are you going to a bar? Can I come along?
sentences.text: Are you going to a bar? Can I come along?

tip: 'How's X coming along?' is the everyday way to ask about progress.

examples: Everybody came together to fix the outage, even people from other teams.
The design is finally coming together after three iterations.
It all came together in the last two days before the launch.
meaning: To unite as a group; or for separate parts to start forming a whole.
tip: 'It's coming together' is a warm way to say a project is taking shape.

examples: She presented the redesign with real conviction.
My conviction is that fewer features will serve users better.
He lacked conviction, so the stakeholders didn't buy the plan.
meaning: A firm belief; or the quality of being confident and certain in what you say.
tip: 'Speak with conviction' = sound sure. Note the legal meaning too: 'a criminal conviction'.

examples: It feels corny to say, but I really love this team.
The onboarding copy is a bit corny; let's make it drier.
Corny as it sounds, the mission is what keeps me here.
heard: It feels so corny to say
meaning: Too sentimental or obvious, in a slightly embarrassing way.
tip: Informal. Saying 'I know it sounds corny, but…' lets you be sincere without sounding naive.

examples: It takes courage to say 'I don't know' in front of the leadership team.
She had the courage to kill her own feature when the data said so.
Curiosity, vulnerability and conviction add up to courage.
meaning: The ability to do something difficult or frightening even though you are afraid.
tip: Collocations: 'have the courage to', 'it takes courage', 'pluck up the courage'.

examples: Let's dissect the funnel and see where people drop off.
We dissected the competitor's onboarding screen by screen.
Don't dissect every word of the feedback; look at the pattern.
meaning: To examine something in great detail, piece by piece.

sentences.corrected: Hi! Today we're here to dissect the new feature since we've received feedback about its quality.
sentences.text: Hi! Today we're here because of the new feature we should dissect as we got feedback about quality

sentences.corrected: We have to dissect this bug report; it's crucial to fix it by Friday.
sentences.text: We have to dissect this bug report, it's crucial to fix it until friday

tip: Pronounced 'dis-SECT'. Slightly clinical; 'break down' is the casual alternative.

examples: Let's flip the question around: what would make users leave?
Flip the layout around so the primary action is on the right.
He flipped the argument around and made it about cost.
meaning: To turn something to the opposite side or reverse the order or perspective.
tip: 'Flip it around' is a handy phrase in brainstorms for changing perspective.

examples: The case study feels formulaic; every section has the same shape.
Interview answers can sound formulaic if you rehearse too much.
Their landing pages are formulaic but they convert well.
meaning: Following a fixed pattern or formula, without originality.
tip: Usually mildly negative. Related: 'cookie-cutter', 'by the numbers'.

examples: That research report is full of gems; read the quotes section.
The Berlin office is a hidden gem for food.
Her Slack messages have gems of advice all over the place.
meaning: Something or someone excellent and valuable, often not widely known.
tip: 'Hidden gem' is the standard collocation. Also used for people: 'he's a gem'.

examples: One engineer with AI tools has way more leverage than before.
We can leverage the existing design system instead of starting from scratch.
Having a working prototype gives you leverage in the roadmap discussion.
heard: One dude have way more leverage than before
meaning: Power to influence a situation; as a verb, to use something to maximum advantage.

sentences.corrected: We have no leverage here, so I presume it's better to get back to work and build a prototype first.
sentences.text: We have no leverage here, I presume is better to get back to work and built a prototype first

tip: The verb 'leverage' is corporate-speak; 'use' is often better. The noun is fine everywhere.

examples: My heart sank when I saw the production error at 6 pm on Friday.
Her heart sort of sank when the feature was cut from the release.
My heart sank a little when I realised I'd shared the wrong file.
meaning: I suddenly felt disappointed or worried.
tip: Past tense 'sank'. Soft, human way to describe a bad moment in a retro.

examples: There's a peculiar bug that only appears on Tuesdays.
Users have a peculiar habit of double-tapping the save button.
The naming convention is peculiar to this codebase.
meaning: Strange or unusual; also, belonging to one particular person or thing.
tip: 'Peculiar to X' = specific to X. On its own it means 'odd', softer than 'weird'.

examples: Mind if I tag along to the customer call? I'd love to listen.
The new hire tagged along to a few design reviews to learn the process.
You can tag along, just stay on mute.
meaning: To go somewhere with someone, usually without being the main participant.
tip: Informal; can imply you weren't really invited, so frame it politely.

examples: Underneath the simple UI there's a lot of complex logic.
Put the helper text underneath the input, not above it.
He seems calm, but underneath he's quite stressed about the deadline.
meaning: Directly below or hidden under something.
tip: Works for both physical position and hidden feelings or systems. 'Beneath' is the more formal twin.

examples: I can vouch for her; we worked together for three years.
I can't vouch for the data, I didn't run the query myself.
The lead vouched for the contractor's work.
meaning: To say from your own experience that someone or something is reliable or true.
tip: Strong word: you put your own credibility behind the claim.

examples: The bug allegedly only happens on Samsung devices; we haven't reproduced it.
Allegedly the vendor fixed the issue in the last release.
He allegedly shipped it without a review.
meaning: Said to be true, but not yet proven.
tip: Legal flavour; used jokingly to show you haven't checked something yourself.

examples: Be assertive about the deadline, but stay open to trade-offs.
She gave assertive, well-reasoned pushback in the planning meeting.
An assertive 'no' now saves a painful 'sorry' later.
meaning: Confident in stating opinions and needs, without being aggressive.
tip: Positive in Anglo work culture; 'aggressive' is the negative version, 'passive' the opposite.

examples: Put the icon beside the label, not above it.
Beside the point: let's get back to the user problem.
She sat beside the PM during the review.
meaning: Next to or at the side of something.
tip: Watch out: 'besides' (with s) means 'in addition / apart from': 'Besides that, the copy needs work.'

examples: When you come off stage after a talk, write down what landed.
I don't want to come off as arrogant in the review.
The joke in the keynote didn't quite come off.
meaning: To leave a stage or surface; also, to give a particular impression, or to succeed.
tip: 'Come off as X' = seem X to others, very useful: 'Did that come off as rude?'

examples: How do you envisage the handoff between design and engineering?
I envisage a single search bar replacing the three filters.
We didn't envisage this many support tickets.
meaning: To imagine or picture something as a future possibility.
tip: British-leaning; Americans say 'envision'. Both are formal and good for strategy talk.

examples: My manager pulled me aside after the meeting to give some feedback.
Pull me aside anytime if something in the process feels off.
She pulled the engineer aside to check the estimate quietly.
meaning: To take someone away from a group to speak with them privately.
tip: Neutral or kind, not necessarily negative. 'Take someone aside' means the same.

examples: Don't be a pushover in scope discussions; the roadmap will eat you.
He's no pushover, he'll ask for the data.
New managers are sometimes pushovers because they want to be liked.
meaning: A person who is easily persuaded or taken advantage of.

sentences.corrected: Be careful with Joe, he's a pushover and can be easily distracted by other people's opinions.
sentences.text: Be carefull with Joe, he's pushover and can be easily distracted by others people opinion

tip: Informal and mildly insulting. Also 'a pushover' can mean something very easy to do.

examples: The design system gives junior designers scaffolding so they can move fast.
Treat the onboarding checklist as scaffolding; remove it once people are confident.
We generated the project scaffolding with a template.
meaning: A temporary structure that supports something while it is being built; in work, the support or structure that helps people learn or deliver.
tip: In tech, 'to scaffold a project' means to generate its basic structure automatically.

examples: We scaled down the launch to two markets after the budget cut.
Let's scale the first version down to the core flow.
The team was scaled down from eight to five people.
meaning: To reduce the size or extent of something.

sentences.corrected: Guys, our product has tons of bugs. We need to think about how to scale down the scope.
sentences.text: Guys, our product have tons of bugs. We need to think how to scale down them

tip: Opposites: 'scale up', 'scale out'. 'Scale back' is a near synonym.

examples: I want to stress that this is a prototype, not the final design.
She stressed the importance of testing with real data.
Let me stress one point: accessibility isn't optional.
meaning: To emphasize something because it is important.
tip: 'I want to stress that…' is a natural way to highlight a key message in a meeting.

examples: The first version of the redesign was too timid; nobody noticed it.
I was a bit timid in my first standups, which is normal.
Don't be timid about asking for context in week one.
meaning: Shy and lacking confidence; easily frightened.
tip: Can describe decisions, not just people: 'a timid rollout'. Opposite: 'bold'.

examples: We'll work it out in the design review tomorrow.
The partnership didn't work out, so we built it in-house.
Give me ten minutes to work out the spacing math.
heard: Work it out / It's not going to work out
meaning: To solve or figure something out; or, of a plan, to succeed in the end.
tip: Two meanings: 'work it out' (solve) and 'it worked out' (ended well). Also 'work out' = exercise.

examples: Low-end Android devices dominate in emerging markets, so performance matters.
Our growth this year came mostly from emerging markets.
Payments UX in emerging markets looks very different.
meaning: A country whose economy is growing fast and becoming more developed.
tip: Also 'emerging technology', 'emerging trend': something new that is becoming important.

examples: Hitting a million users was the inflection point for the company.
We're at an inflection point: either invest in the platform or keep patching.
Her inflection made the question sound like a statement.
meaning: A moment when a trend changes direction significantly; in speech, the rise and fall of your voice.
tip: 'Inflection point' is business jargon from mathematics; it signals a big strategic shift.

examples: Can you pull together a quick summary of the research by Thursday?
The team really pulled together during the incident.
I'll pull the screens together into one Figma page.
meaning: To gather things into one place; or for people to cooperate in a difficult time.
tip: 'Pull together a deck / a summary / a plan' is extremely common in work English.

examples: When the product was shut down, it felt like our identity was ripped away.
The redesign ripped away features that power users relied on.
Don't rip away the old flow overnight; migrate people gradually.
meaning: To remove something suddenly and violently.
tip: Emotional and dramatic. Softer options: 'take away', 'remove', 'phase out'.

examples: The referral feature caused sign-ups to take off.
The product didn't take off until they fixed onboarding.
I'm taking off early today for a doctor's appointment.
meaning: To suddenly become successful or popular; also, to leave, or for a plane to depart.
tip: 'Take off' (succeed) vs 'take time off' (holiday) vs 'take off a hat'. Context decides.

examples: The offsite had a convivial atmosphere, lots of laughter over dinner.
He's a convivial host who makes new hires feel welcome.
The retro was surprisingly convivial for a failed launch.
meaning: Friendly, lively, and enjoyable, usually describing an atmosphere or a person.
tip: Formal and a little literary; 'friendly' or 'warm' is what you'd say in a standup.

examples: Let's not wallow in the failed A/B test; what did we learn?
He wallowed in self-pity for a day, then rewrote the proposal.
Retros should reflect, not wallow.
meaning: To stay in an unhappy feeling and almost enjoy it, instead of moving on.
tip: Almost always 'wallow in X': self-pity, misery, nostalgia. Mildly negative.

examples: There's no evidence whatsoever that users want this feature.
I have no objection whatsoever to moving the meeting.
The change had no impact whatsoever on conversion.
meaning: At all; used after a negative to make it stronger.
tip: Always after 'no / nothing / none / any': 'none whatsoever'.

examples: We'll build out the component library over the next two quarters.
Let's build the happy path first and build it out from there.
They're building out a research team in Berlin.
meaning: To develop something further until it is complete or larger.
tip: Very common in product teams: 'build out a feature / a team / a process'.

examples: Small daily reviews compound into real fluency within months.
Design debt compounds if nobody pays it down.
Compound learning is why writing things down beats cramming.
meaning: To grow by building on what already exists, so each gain makes the next one bigger.
tip: From 'compound interest'. 'It compounds' is a favourite phrase in startup talk.

examples: Can someone help him out with the Figma permissions?
I helped out on the support rota during the incident.
Thanks for helping me out with the deck last night.
meaning: To help someone, especially with a specific task or in a difficult moment.

sentences.corrected: I see you're struggling with this task. Could I help you out?
sentences.text: I see you're struggling with this task. Could I help you out?

tip: 'Help out' is more casual and friendly than plain 'help'.

examples: The surprise question knocked me off my stride for a moment.
Don't let one tough review knock you off stride.
Constant Slack pings knock the whole team off stride.
meaning: To interrupt someone so they lose their rhythm or confidence.

sentences.corrected: Sorry, but you absolutely knocked me off my stride. Can I start over?
sentences.text: Sorry but you absolutely knocked me off, can I start over?

tip: Also 'throw someone off', 'put someone off their game'. Recover with: 'Sorry, where was I?'

examples: Good teammates look out for each other during crunch.
Look out for the edge case where the name field is empty.
She's always looking out for the junior designers.
meaning: To take care of someone; or to watch carefully for something.
tip: 'Look out!' alone is a warning. 'Look out for' is caring or alert; 'look for' is just searching.

examples: As a staff designer, ask yourself: are you rowing or steering today?
In week one you'll mostly be rowing; steering comes once you know the team.
Managers who keep rowing never find time to steer.
meaning: A leadership metaphor: doing the work yourself (rowing) versus setting direction for others (steering).
tip: Useful for talking about seniority and delegation without jargon.

examples: Activation ticked up two points after we shortened the form.
Churn is ticking up in the SMB segment; worth a look.
The number ticked up overnight, nothing dramatic.
meaning: To increase by a small amount.
tip: Opposite 'tick down'. For big changes use 'jump', 'spike', 'surge'.

examples: Let's dive into the analytics before we redesign anything.
I'll dive into the codebase this week to understand the constraints.
She sat down with the users and dived into their daily routines.
heard: Sitting down and diving into people
meaning: To start examining or doing something with energy and in depth.
tip: 'Deep dive' is the noun: 'Let's do a deep dive on checkout next sprint.'

examples: The icons don't line up with the text baseline.
I've lined up five user interviews for next week.
Our roadmap doesn't line up with marketing's launch dates.
meaning: To arrange things in a row or in agreement; to organize or schedule something in advance.
tip: Design sense: 'line up' = align. Planning sense: 'line up a meeting / a candidate'.

examples: Most users pass through the pricing page without reading it.
Every request passes through the gateway first.
Design feedback passes through the PM before it reaches engineering.
meaning: To go through a place or stage without stopping; in tech, to forward data unchanged.
tip: Noun form 'a pass-through' is common in engineering and in finance.

examples: Can you pull up the dashboard so we can look at the numbers?
Let me pull it up in Figma, one second.
Hold on, I'll pull up the ticket.
meaning: To open or display something on a screen; also, to stop a vehicle, or to improve a bad result.
tip: The everyday way to say 'open on screen' in meetings: 'pull up the doc'.

examples: The NGO's app supports refugee resettlement in Germany.
Resettlement programs need multilingual onboarding by default.
Her research covered resettlement experiences in Berlin.
meaning: The process of moving people to live in a new place, often after displacement.
tip: Formal, social-policy word. For your own move abroad, 'relocation' is the normal term.

examples: We'll talk about pricing shortly, let me finish the user flow first.
The recording will be shared shortly after the call.
Shortly after launch, the first bug reports came in.
heard: We will talk about that shortly
meaning: Soon; in a short time.
tip: 'Shortly' means 'soon', not 'briefly'. To mean 'in few words', say 'briefly'.

examples: The primary button should stand out from the secondary ones.
One insight stood out from the interviews: people fear losing data.
Her portfolio stands out because every case shows the trade-offs.
meaning: To be clearly better or more noticeable than others.
tip: Adjective 'standout': 'a standout candidate'. Phrase: 'stand out from the crowd'.

examples: Let's start off with a quick round of updates.
I'll start it off by sharing the research goals.
The project started off well but slowed down in Q3.
meaning: To begin something, or to begin in a particular way.

sentences.corrected: To start off with, here's our meeting agenda.
sentences.text: To start off with, here's our meetings agends

tip: 'Kick off' is the more energetic synonym: 'kick off the meeting'.

examples: Strategy changes take months to trickle down to individual tickets.
The new values trickled down from leadership to the teams.
Insights from research rarely trickle down to engineering on their own.
meaning: To spread slowly from the top to lower levels.
tip: Often slightly skeptical, from 'trickle-down economics'. 'Trickle' = a thin, slow flow.

examples: I had a chip on my shoulder after being passed over for the lead role.
He works with a chip on his shoulder, always proving he belongs.
Drop the chip on your shoulder; nobody here doubts you.
meaning: A lasting feeling of resentment or of having something to prove.
tip: Can be negative (bitterness) or admiring (drive). Often 'with a chip on his shoulder'.

examples: Let's peel apart the two problems: slow load time and confusing copy.
When you peel apart the metric, most of the growth is one region.
The team peeled the monolith apart into services.
meaning: To separate layers or parts carefully, often to understand them.
tip: Similar: 'tease apart', 'untangle', 'peel back the layers'.

examples: From a design standpoint, the second option is simpler to learn.
From this standpoint, the delay actually helped us.
Consider it from the support team's standpoint.
meaning: A particular way of looking at a situation; a point of view.
tip: Pattern: 'from a(n) X standpoint' where X is business, technical, legal, user.

examples: You want to tie the product to people's daily routine.
Tie each design decision to a user problem in your case study.
Bonuses are tied to team goals, not individual output.
heard: You want tie product to daily Routine of the people
meaning: To connect one thing to another so they depend on each other.
tip: Passive 'is tied to' is very common: 'retention is tied to notifications'.
